text: Mind just blown by hidden excel trick  I have been using excel for about 25 years now and just had my mind blown by this trick that to be honest with you I wish I had known a lot sooner. Maybe you already knew it but I just found out about it. If you are like me that post screenshots of drawing details and paste it all over your spreadsheets, you are going to have images floating around like crazy. I wanted the ability for the screenshot to popup when I need to see the image and hide when I dont. Doing a little research on youtube I found this guy that showed how this can be done with the New Note option on a cell. If you right click on any cell, you will see the NEW NOTE option. When you click on it the small text area for the note will appear. He said if you hover over the note area and right click and click on FORMAT COMMENT only the FONT tab will open. BUT and here is the trick, But if you hover over the BORDER of the NOTE (not inside the note but on the BORDER; you will notice when you are on the border when your cursor changes to a cross of arrows ) and right click and click on FORMAT COMMENT, then not only the FONT tab will appear but a bunch of other tabs too. Click on COLORS AND LINES, under fill > Color click on down arrow, then Fill Effects. Then on picture > select your picture then OK. And bam there you have it. an image that pops up only when you hover a cell. leaving the lock picture aspect ratio uncheck will allow you to size the window later to the actual size of the image. Now I wont have floating images all around my spreadsheets. Super usefull when you want to see a detail on a drawing really quick, without having to switch to bluebeam or your pdf viewer to see it. or any image you would like really. On a sidenote, you can quickly create images from your PDF with the snipping tool. JPG format works great. Edit1 = BONUS TIP = With the snipping tool PNG and GIF images work as well.

text: AI in preconstruction (scope notes, bid-leveling)  There's so much hype around AI, but I genuinely believe AI can introduce some much needed improvements in preconstruction and this is something that really excites me. For the last 4 weeks, I've been exploring ideas around getting AI to help me generate better scope-notes / line-items. I wanted to share some of my findings w/ the community. The ultimate vision I like scifi-stuff so I started wondering if we could build an intelligent AI-assistant that automatically ingests plans issued by an architect and instantly does the following? Recommended subcontractors : What subcontractors are required on this project based on scope outlined in plans? Imagine a world where GCs can go from plans to a list of relevant subcontractors within seconds. Line items : Analyze key notes, general notes & schedules to understand scope of work per trade and instantly generate a list of required line-items for a GC to review. Imagine if every GC had an AI-assistant to generate a first-draft for bid-leveling / scope-sheet and their job was to review and make changes. Highlight gotchas: Call out important details to watch out for (e.g. material substitutions, exclusions, inclusions, special materials). Addendas: What are the exact changes that have occurred on the plans? How does this fit into context with every trade? A GC shouldn’t have to compare new and old versions of plans side-by-side to understand these changes. Instead an AI should instantly call out the changes and provide notes & context. TLDR - AI shows promise, but there's still a lot of hard-technical challenges Here's a snapshot of HVAC floor plans from one of my projects. ​ https://preview.redd.it/vn62hw40c1ib1.png?width=2154&format=png&auto=webp&s=07322fbe2242bd679dd723869f59dc5d8b55d15d If you feed this input to an AI / Large-language model, it can start to effectively summarize this info into structured format. https://preview.redd.it/oew00go5c1ib1.png?width=1188&format=png&auto=webp&s=860b592c7f74268e21df81aa89a2b4d7a607fb01 In fact, I was able to generate a bunch of scope notes for number of trades (demo, HVAC, etc). You can see for yourself via this video! https://www.loom.com/share/3602d5b464de4d4798559b98150a0880?sid=2db96f8e-27fc-486a-af14-764bec6fe506 ​ Bold Prediction (old world vs new world) The old world of preconstruction A GC has to look through a big PDF of construction blueprints and do these things. Sub selection : Look through 100-page plans, identify all scopes that are needed manually (e.g. electrical, mechanical, drywall), invite subs Scope sheet : Analyze key notes, general notes & schedules to understand scope of work per trade and instantly generate scope / line-items Material sheets: Same process as above Specs / gotchas / addendas: Compare plans side by side, scan a bunch of construction text Highlight gotchas: Call out important details to watch out for (e.g. material substitutions, exclusions, inclusions, special materials). Addendas: What are the exact changes that have occurred on the plans? How does this fit into context with every trade? A GC shouldn’t have to compare new and old versions of plans side-by-side to understand these changes. New world of precon (w/ AI) Sub selection: Instantly call out relevant trades -> share list for GC to review Scope sheet: Translate plans, identify line-items, transcribe into an excel sheet automatically --> share w/ GC to review Material sheets / specs / gotchas / addendas: Provide relevant context, call out changes --> share w/ GC to review Where AI fails Despite the excitement, I think the technology still has major limitations. For example, I uploaded entire blueprints to chatGPT and Claude and just prompted the AI to do various stuff (e.g give me line items for electrical, etc). Results were stupidly awful, which means AI is not SO SMART that it can fully automate the job of an estimator. Large plans: When the plans are large, the AI models cannot detect all scope. It just can't process all this information. Different formats: Plans come in various formats, PDFs, images, multiple files. Sheets are a messy compilation of general-notes, product-specs, diagrams, key notes, addenda clouds, tables. Even the best AI models can’t understand this complexity out-of-the-box. Lost Context: Plans are rich with information (schedules, specs, key notes), but AI models see all this as 1-blob of text. Even something as simple, give me all materials that are spec'd on this set of plans is difficult. That said, you can start to get around these problems by making it easier for AI to understand your blueprints. Some techniques i found useful were Give AI context on your project Limit the tasks to just a single section of the plans (e.g. electrical, mechanical, architectural) Use some computer vision to tag material schedules Use OCR to standardize the text on blueprints When you do this, the results start to look pretty good (as shown in my video). E.g. using computer vision to segment blueprints to help AI Building a community of GCs / subs excited about AI This AI-application really excites me. I'd love to build a small-community of GC/sub precon professionals who are interested in exploring AI ideas on the side (e.g. applying AI to scope generation, bid-leveling, conceptual designs). We can build some prototypes, exchange ideas and see where these ideas go. If these ideas excite you, drop me a DM or a comment and we can start an email-group. Would also love to hear what other people have seen w/ AI applied to precon / construction (pitfalls, limitations, exciting applications, etc).

text: I analyzed Texas (TxDOT) bid data for 4,583 projects. Here's what I found.  Hey all, I've been poking around public bid data lately, and figured you might find some of it interesting. Pulled the Texas Department of Transportation (TxDOT) bid tabulation dataset: 732,235 18,171 bids (see edit 2) across 4,583 projects from Jan 2024 through now. Here's what jumped out. Win rates: For contractors with 10+ bids on record: - Median win rate: 23.2% - 44.2% of contractors win less than 1 in 5 - Only 20.2% win more than half their bids So if you're hitting 20-25%, you're right at the median. Better than nearly half the field. This is the interesting part. Of all losing bids 83,292 lost by 5% or less. That burns!: | Gap to Winner | % of Losses | Raw Count | | ≤1% | 3.0% | 17,195 bids | | ≤5% | 14.8% | 83,292 bids | | ≤10% | 29.3% | 165,387 bids | The median loss margin was 17.7% so half of all losses were closer than that, half were further. text: An in-depth guide for finding subs in 24-hrs  Hello construction reddit, I see a lot of posts from GCs asking “how do I find subs to bid?”. This is especially hard for GCs that are moving to new markets because they have no existing relationships (e.g. traveling GC that is expanding operations from CA to NV). A lot of posts & blogs provide generic strategies like Use google maps Use bid platforms like building connected, smartbid Drive around in a truck and talk to subs Ask for referrals IMO these solutions are surface-level and don’t truly solve the problem. A few months ago, I saw an opportunity to build sublists quickly using techniques common in the software industry (web-scraping, programmatic emailing, machine learning) and it’s been working well. Today, I want to share insights on how to build sublists with the community because it might be useful to other GCs. Background For context, I built company that makes bid-management tools for commercial trade contractors. We have a sales team that needs high-quality commercial subcontractor leads. Sourcing these leads proved difficult. We scraped databases (BlueBook, BuildingConnected), but we ran into so many data problems (subs in wrong trades, wrong contact info) We’d use google maps, but half the results were residential leads and useless for us We’d purchase lists from companies like ZoomInfo, but they missed a lot of important construction-specific attributes that sales needed (e.g. trade, union/non-union) So we built an in-house solution to generate sublists quickly. Then one day, a GC friend saw this and asked if he could use this for one of his projects. He’s the chief estimator GC that builds luxury retail chains (Tiffany’s, Dior, Ralph Lauren) and they travel all over the country. It turns out it’s critical for them to build high-quality sublists quickly in new territories as well. He inspired me to write this post b/c he found our tool useful. Problem Let’s say you’re a GC that focuses on luxury retail work in Los Angeles, CA, but you’ve won a negotiated job in Las Vegas, NV. How would you generate a list of NV subs that would be a good fit for the job? Our goal was to generate a list of subs with this information Trades performed Area of work MWBE status Union / non-union status Average project size Past projects Estimating decision makers (emails & phone #s) Failed Solutions We tried a lot of methods, but they all failed for different reasons. Google maps + calls Using google maps, we would run a query “electrical contractors in Las Vegas”, then research their website and manually call each sub to ask if they had done luxury retail. The problem is it took days and hours just to prep a sublist. As a small estimating team we didn’t have the manpower to call the thousands of subs and vet them. BuildingConnected & Planhub & other bid platforms BuildingConnected & Planhub seemed like a nice solution because they have a large database of subs. We ran into two problems. First, the information was out-of-date (subs listed under wrong trades, contact information was wrong) which caused us to have to manually fix a lot of the data. Secondly, we’d send a generic ITB and barely get any responses because in any competitive market, subs don’t respond to generic bid-platform ITBs. Ask for referrals We’d ask for referrals from 1-2 local subs and then slowly work the network. For example, we’d talk to a manufacturer’s rep, get 1-3 HVAC subs. Then we’d ask these HVAC subs for recs for drywall and electrical and glass subs, rinse and repeat. This was great, but it was still incredibly time-consuming. Again manpower issue. Our approach (web-scraping, machine learning, programmatic emails) The definition of a great sublist is simple. Find every single subcontractor in an area Get accurate, up-to-date on the sub (e.g. trades performed, MWBE, union/non-union) Find the right decision maker My challenge was to build a way so that our estimating team could push a button and get accurate sublists without doing any work. The first thing I did was break down this challenge into mini-problems. (A) Map the universe of subs in an area The first challenge was to find every single construction sub in a market. To do that, I built a web-scraper that would pull a sub’s name and website URL from a few construction databases, which publicly list subs. BlueBook Association websites for specialty trades like NECA, AWCI In addition, google maps has an API so you can run automated queries like “electrical sub in <zip code>”. I created a list of common trades we needed and every zip code in the nation to build a gigantic list of subs. If a sub had a website or some internet presence, these methods would find it. Now I have a gigantic list of every sub in the U.S. (B) Scrape each website, clean the data & get accurate information about the sub A gigantic list of subs and websites isn’t useful and there’s a lot of problems. For example, the sub’s website may be out-of-date, it may be a manufacturer’s rep rather than a sub. Therefore, the second challenge was to clean the data and make it useful for bidding outreach. To do that, I built a web-scraping tool that would visit website-by-website and extract the following information Trades performed Area of work MWBE status Union / non-union status Average project size Past projects Estimating decision makers (emails & phone #s) Phone #s Estimating email Here are some examples of the techniques i used Predict the trade based on the description on the home-page using machine learning (e.g. if the word electrical is common on a home-page, predict that it’s an electrical sub) Extract basic info (e.g. location, emails, phone numbers) using web-scraping Look for specific keywords like MWBE, union using web-scraping The output is a clean excel sheet with every sub in our market, enriched with key information. (C) Get contact information Armed with a clean sublist, the next challenge was to find the decision maker at each company and his or her contact information. Unfortunately, most websites don’t list the chief estimator’s contact information and just have generic emails like [info@subcontractor.com](mailto:info@subcontractor.com). In our experience, if you just blindly send a bid to a generic email you’ll never get a response. To start, I used a tool called phantom buster which would allow me to extract employee and job-titles from a company’s linkedin. Then I used a software script to guess each person’s email and use third-party email verification to confirm the email is correct. By using this process, we now had direct contacts at each company and their email. (D) Fill in the data gaps with programmatic emails However, not everyone in construction is on linkedin, let alone chief estimators. So for the companies where we didn’t find the right estimating decision maker, we would directly email a contact at the company with a templated email asking for the decision maker. In this email, I would add a bit of salesmanship (introduce myself, introduce the project and the estimated revenue). Most people would manually write every email, but we used tools like Lemlist that basically allow you to send a personal-email from your domain, but do this in a programmatic way. This allows you to email 100s of companies simultaneously. We gathered these responses and added it to our list of contacts. For the companies that never responded, we’d directly call and ask for the decision maker. Impact for GC friend In summary, we built a tool that breaks down generating sublists into a few components. Finding all subs Vetting subs programmatically using their website Finding up-to-date contact info for these subs Reaching out via emails & calls for info that we’re missing Per my GC friend, this tool has given them a way to generate fast-sublists so they can be more strategic about getting bid coverage since they’re no longer blindly calling every sub, but just prioritizing the ones that are a good fit using the data we’ve scraped. For the GCs, I’m curious to hear how you guys generate sublists at your company because I’m looking to improve this tool.
